body_text: Sometimes it’s important to remember what sport you’re playing, as recently a hard-fought Brazilian youth soccer game devolved into a piqued MLB game or relatively subdued and reasonable ice hockey game. The game became a brawl that resulted in a world-record 53 red cards that ejected 43 players, 8 coaches, and two team board members from the fight on the field. In any company, it’s always nice to know the board has got your back, I guess. On Friday, stocks rebounded somewhat from Thursday’s $2.5T Nasdaq bloodbath, but overall finished a volatile week in the red. Last week the midterms resulted in a sweeping victory for congressional Democrats, and in the days that followed it became clear that what that means for the market is obvious, uncomplicated, and straightforward: nobody really knows exactly what that meant for the market, it’s very complicated and in no way straightforward. The day after the midterms stocks surged, the day after that the Nasdaq took a historic dump, and then the day after that things bounced back a bit. The upshot of last week in the aggregate was down a bit, but sector-by-sector things are not so simple. Companies used the opportunity of the market chaos to rip off some band-aids. Microsoft made a flurry of announcements that amounted to a paring back deals with the external providers of compute — chastising the neoclouds and pulling the plug on a compute rental provided by Oracle — that certainly sent a chill through the parts of the AI trade that serve those interests. Tesla managed to pop 5% on Friday in a week that was, electorally speaking, a fundamental rejection of the political project of Elon Musk. It did so by announcing that it was going to stop bleeding money out making Cybertrucks, and instead throw those production lines towards making Cybercabs. There was lots of more general house cleaning, such as Waymo announcing it would soon soon be done working with Uber , Oracle canceling a chip lease agreement with Tencent, Kraft Heinz planning to sell off its coffee business, and CVS spinning off… CVS. All the kind of news you drop when the market is so crazy you can’t really figure out what’s moving what. In all, the week was less about the end of this trade or the start of that, but more of a rotation. Hyperscalers Microsoft, Amazon and Google all finished the week up; if the week revealed anything, it’s that having existing datacenters in the ground is important, and that if you’re a company planning on putting more in the ground, well, maybe you should let Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa save you from yourself, and just go ahead and give that money to shareholders instead. Meanwhile, some of the biggest losers of the week were the companies that were riding the high of those companies capex moves. Some of the biggest drops of the week were storage chips ( Seagate , Sandisk ) and the connectivity and so-called “picks-and-shovels” of the data center build-out ( Lumentum , Marvell , Astera Labs , Micron ). Speaking of picks and shovels, another trade indicates how the midterms’ pushback on new data center construction has manifested in markets. Sure, companies like Caterpillar dropped, but homebuilders gained. Caterpillar supplies the literal picks and shovels of the data center build-out, and with that potentially slowing down, so did it. On the other hand, homebuilders that have had an exhausting time competing with data center construction for capital, materials, and labor surged, with Toll Brothers , DR Horton and PulteGroup all finishing the week up. A nota bene on PulteGroup that shows how weird this market has been. The large residential construction company was a huge winner of the week, spiking 8% between Tuesday's close and Wednesday's open, finishing the week up nearly 5%, now that Democrats will finally have a hand in steering housing policy. This is a somewhat ironic market rebuke of the administration, given that the grandson of the company's founder is currently serving as Trump's director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency and head of Freddie Mac. My colleague Luke Kawa, who writes the brilliant EntryPoint newsletter that goes in-depth on this stuff, is fond of the aphorism “my capex spending is your profit margins,” and that has been on display this past week. The AI trade will continue, but the beneficiaries of that trade — and the ultimate total addressable market of the business — will remain in flux. A few weeks ago, we wrote about the CoreWeave debt contretemps, and we made the point that just because a company got a lot of money doesn’t mean it’s gonna be one of the winners of the AI trade, writing “Just because your business model was the beating heart of the AI industry in 2026 doesn’t prevent you from being the bloated, doomed appendix of the AI industry in 2032. Not every buzzy well-funded company’s gonna make it.” Last week, if anything, confirmed that the future indeed won’t be evenly distributed. Okay, Uber might have been a “ little bit of a crapshoot ” for riders looking to book a robotaxi, per Waymo’s co-CEO. Yes, notching just four ride bookings via AI agents during the Halloween period probably wasn’t the spooky season performance it had hoped for. And alright, the company’s president defecting to OpenAI might have added to what hasn’t, on the surface, been a great news week for Uber. Park all of that for just a minute, however, and some of the numbers out of Uber’s third-quarter report earlier this week must still have been enough for execs still at the company to cheer at least a little. Although revaluing equity investments weighed on earnings to the point of missing, Uber revenues rose 9.6% from last year to hit $14.77 billion and beat estimates. Trips taken on Uber — that is, slightly confusingly, the sum of trips taken in Uber cars and total deliveries made on Uber Eats — hit a staggering 4.06 billion in the quarter. That tally means that each of Uber’s 215 million monthly active platform users must have ordered a taxi, or a taxi for their burrito , just shy of 19 times (more than six times each month) on average last quarter. Imagine how many more the company could’ve clocked without the driver shortages in India, Canada, and Brazil that it also disclosed this quarter . For those of you who see that trip figure and still assume Uber mostly functions as a ride-hailing service, the company’s split on gross bookings, which rose 20% from last year to reach almost $60 billion in the third quarter, might not be what you expect… and the balance might not have been how you thought for a while now. Since Delivery gross bookings value overtook Mobility during the pandemic era — remember? Not many of us were taking taxis and a lot of us were getting stuff delivered because there was nothing else to do? — there’s really not been a huge margin separating the two in either direction. In the last quarter, Uber booked $29.5 billion from rides and just around $1 billion less from its Delivery segment; its Freight division, which brought in $1.8 billion, still clearly has a ways to go. While some of the more eye-catching Uber news this week might not have looked great on paper, the billions of trips and hundreds of millions of riders and users that the company notches each quarter undoubtedly softened the blow. title: 🌊 The blue wave washed data centers away
body_text: Sweetgreen is in a tough spot. The premium-priced slop bowl seller has recently been caught in a vortex of rising labor costs, increasing wholesale food prices, and choppy sales. The company is eager to be known as something other than the place that sells $20+ salads. Instead, the Wall Street Journal reports that Sweetgreen is eager to be known as the place with the $15 wraps. The company is also beefing up portion sizes and making build-your-own salad pricing more transparent in an effort to woo customers. Perhaps the only people more dejected by Tuesday’s election results than Republican politicians are data center developers. Data centers – the kilowatt-sucking warehouses filled with server racks and cooling equipment – were on the ballot across the country and the results were emphatic: Voters don’t like data centers. They really really don’t like data centers. In the 41 local races across the country where a data center moratorium, new regulations, or a specific project itself was on the ballot, voters weighed in against data centers 40 times, Semafor reports . Those election night results don’t come out of the blue, of course. Back in May, Gallup found that 71% of Americans opposed data center construction in their area. To put that 71% opposition figure in context, building new data centers is just about as unpopular as releasing the Epstein files is popular ( 75% of Americans support the latter.) In terms of the market reaction to voters’ data center displeasure, it would be easy to look at the post election rally in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 and think that meant that investors expected little to no hiccups in the AI trade, and specifically, the data center trade, to proceed with little to no hiccups while Democrats control the House and Senate. Looking a bit more granularly at the market reaction, that doesn’t seem to be the case. While the broad indices are indeed up, the VanEck Semiconductor ETF and the RoundHill Memory ETF – which as their names indicate, respectively track semiconductor and memory storage shares – ended the day in the red. Nvidia , Broadcom , and Marvell all tumbled. (In a sign of just how negative investor sentiment is, AMD printed strong earnings and boosted guidance and ended the day barely eking out a gain.) And who among the AI trade gained on the day? The hyperscalers – Amazon , Google , Meta , Microsoft – were all in the green. SpaceX was conspicuously down, as investors reassessed the downsides of Elon Musk’s close alliance with the President Trump and the failure of Musk’s interventions on behalf of the GOP in Texas’s statewide races. What investors are saying, in a sense, is that if right now you have an already operating data center, it just got more valuable . And if your business is selling stuff to build not-yet-existing data centers, that business just got on balance a little less profitable going forward. As Bloomberg’s Joe Weisenthal put it , the “[Meta Hyperion] campus in Louisiana might be able to charge some pretty high rents.” The massive data center build out in recent years across the Sun Belt in particular was done in large part with full industry enmeshment with the national and state Republican party. That strategy will now largely be unavailable. However, in a purely analytical way – dare we mention game theory ? – despite the tables being fully turned, that strategy had a certain logic. Indeed, if you were in charge of a hyperscaler or an AI lab with an interest in seeing data centers getting built, being as close as possible to Trump and the GOP may have made sense. Assuming a blue wave was coming and there was nothing really that you could do about it, Trump and the GOP were the path to getting the most compute online while you could. Any data center that wasn’t already up and running on Monday has a lower chance of becoming operational and a longer lead time with higher costs if it does. The challenge that the entire data center and AI industry must now reckon with is the blue wave did indeed happen, and Democrats will (accurately!) view their anti-data center campaign messaging as key in helping them win. An industry not used to oversight or much, if any, national-level regulation will now be a key regulatory and investigation target of a party emboldened by a historic win. In response, OpenAI has already decided to rebrand data centers as “ compute campuses .” I’d hazard to predict that won’t be enough to turn the anti-data center tide. 🏈TNF: The Jacksonville Jaguars are a surprise favorite in a Thursday night matchup against the Baltimore Ravens, thanks largely to the likely season-ending thumb injury of Baltimore’s star quarterback Lamar Jackson on Sunday.
